title: The Letter of Little Hawley
premise: Mirabel Kavanagh, a night-shift taxi dispatcher in the fading town of Little Hawley, has spent years solving deaths the police mislabeled as accidents, working alone and leaving anonymous tips. When a drowned woman is found wearing clothes stolen from his own closet, he realizes someone is staging a frame that mirrors his private methods — and that the killer has access to the very case files he once studied. As the statute of limitations closes on a decades-old death that anchors everything, Mirabel must ally with the skeptical detective who once dismissed his tips and confront the retired evidence clerk who has been quietly 'correcting' Little Hawley's history for thirty years. In the end, Mirabel chooses truth over loyalty, exposing the killer and his own complicity in staying silent, and finally steps out of the shadows to be seen.
about_author: Paloma Sandoval is a former small-town court stenographer who spent eleven years transcribing testimony in cases that never made the news. She writes mysteries about the people who notice everything and are believed by no one.

chapters.title: The Quiet Frequency
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. A slow night at the dispatch desk introduces his rituals: mapping calls, cross-referencing obituaries, the anonymous tips he's mailed over the years. When a call comes in about a body at Miller's Pond, he recognizes the address from a case he once flagged. The beat is quiet dread — the feeling that his invisibility is about to end.

chapters.title: Dressed in My Life
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV, with a brief shift to Detective Ada Ruiz. The drowned woman is wearing Mirabel's own jacket and scarf, items reported stolen weeks ago. Ruiz, who once dismissed his tips as crank mail, is assigned the case and finds his name in the old files. The beat is violation — a stranger wearing his identity like a costume.

chapters.title: Three Accidents, One Hand
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. He lays out his private archive: three deaths he solved, all ruled accidents, all tied to the same retired evidence clerk, Edmund Voss. He realizes the new victim, Lorna Pike, had recently requested a copy of a 1992 case file — the one that started everything. The beat is the cold clarity of a pattern finally visible.

chapters.title: The Statute's Shadow
chapters.summary: Ruiz's POV. Ruiz reviews the 1992 file and finds pages subtly altered — dates shifted, a witness statement softened. The statute of limitations on the original obstruction expires in nineteen days. She visits Mirabel unannounced, neither arrest nor ally. The beat is wary triangulation: two people who need each other and hate it.

chapters.title: What Lorna Knew
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. He retraces Lorna's last week: she was a records assistant who'd found a discrepancy in the 1992 evidence log and told one person — her supervisor, who reports to Voss. Mirabel realizes the frame isn't just a frame; it's a message that Voss knows exactly who's been sending anonymous tips. The beat is the vertigo of being hunted by someone who studied him first.

chapters.title: Closet of Evidence
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. He catalogs everything stolen from his apartment and finds one item unaccounted for: his father's old taxi logbook from 1992, which he'd never connected to anything. Flipping through it, he finds his father drove the witness home the night of the original death. The beat is grief reopening — his father's death that year may not have been an accident either.

chapters.title: Nineteen Days
chapters.summary: Ruiz's POV. Ruiz formally reopens the 1992 case over her captain's objections and is warned off by the town attorney. She notices the file's chain of custody passes through Voss's records office for thirty years — meaning every 'corrected' document is technically his sworn testimony. The beat is institutional pressure and the first flicker of trust in Mirabel.

chapters.title: The Fare That Never Logged
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. He interviews the surviving witness from 1992, an old woman in a care home who recites a story word-for-word — a rehearsed statement. But she calls his father by a nickname no stranger would know. The beat is tenderness and horror braided together: she's been protected and imprisoned by the same kindness.

chapters.title: A Tip Signed by Me
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. An anonymous tip arrives at the police station — in Mirabel's exact style, phrasing, even his typewriter's worn 'e' — implicating him in Lorna's death. The killer isn't just framing him; he's impersonating his method. Ruiz shows Mirabel the letter and asks the only question that matters: 'How many did you actually solve?' The beat is exposure.

chapters.title: Confession by Dispatch Tape
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV, intercut with Ruiz's. Mirabel plays Ruiz his dispatch recordings from the night of Lorna's death: a taxi was ordered to the pond from Voss's office phone, then canceled ninety seconds later. It proves Voss lured her — but the tape's existence also proves Mirabel surveilled the town for years. The beat is a bargain struck in the dark.

chapters.title: The Loyalist
chapters.summary: Voss's POV, first time. Voss reflects on thirty years of 'protecting' Little Hawley — burying the 1992 death of a beloved doctor to save the town's hospital from scandal, and later silencing anyone who dug. He regards Mirabel almost fondly, a student he never knew he had. The beat is chilling self-righteousness; the reader sees the killer's logic whole.

chapters.title: Twelve Days
chapters.summary: Ruiz's POV. With the statute clock at twelve days, Ruiz petitions to preserve the case past expiration and is denied. She and Mirabel go off-book, pulling Voss's personnel history: he was the responding officer in 1992, the man who wrote 'accident' before the ambulance arrived. The beat is momentum — the case becoming a race.

chapters.title: The Witness Who Remembers Wrong
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. He returns to the care home and, using his father's logbook, gently walks the old witness through the real night. Her rehearsed story cracks: the doctor was alive when Voss arrived alone. She's been 'corrected' so long she can't tell memory from instruction. The beat is heartbreak — truth damaged almost past repair by loyalty.

chapters.title: Frame Job, Second Draft
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Someone breaks into his apartment and leaves the missing logbook page — the one proving his father's last fare — arranged like a gift. The killer is toying with him, offering pieces, keeping the game alive past the point of necessity. Mirabel understands: Voss doesn't want to win, he wants an audience. The beat is revulsion and a terrible insight.

chapters.title: Eight Days, Two Traps
chapters.summary: Ruiz's POV. Ruiz and Mirabel design a trap: feed Voss a fabricated discrepancy in the 1992 file and see which document gets 'corrected' overnight. The bait is planted. That night, the records room light burns until 3 a.m. The beat is coiled anticipation — the hunters finally setting terms.

chapters.title: The Correction
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. They catch Voss's hand in the file — but not Voss. It's his protégé, a young clerk who genuinely believes he's preserving the town's peace. The protégé breaks and describes Voss's 'archive': a private room of every altered record, kept like relics. The beat is the machinery of loyalty laid bare.

chapters.title: Five Days
chapters.summary: Ruiz's POV. The protégé's statement is shaky and inadmissible; Voss's lawyer moves to quash everything, and the captain suspends Ruiz. Voss sends Mirabel a taxi voucher — a summons. The beat is despair closing in, the law itself now the obstacle to justice.

chapters.title: Miller's Pond, After Midnight
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. He goes alone to the pond, as summoned. Voss confesses with terrible serenity: the doctor's death, his father's 'accident,' Lorna — each a correction. He offers Mirabel partnership: together they could keep fixing the town. Mirabel, wearing a wire, lets him say Lorna's name. The beat is the moral crux — justice offered as complicity.

chapters.title: What the Tape Couldn't Hold
chapters.summary: Ruiz's POV. The wire fails — the pond's cold killed the battery. Voss walks. But Mirabel, anticipating this, had also recited the confession into the old dispatch system, timestamped and archived on the taxi company's servers. Ruiz retrieves it. The beat is a breath held and released: the town's own infrastructure becomes the witness.

chapters.title: The Last Correction
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Two days before the statute expires, Ruiz arrests Voss for Lorna's murder; the archived dispatch tape and the protégé's testimony give the DA enough to charge the 1992 death as well. Voss, unrepentant, asks Mirabel only one question: whether the town was better with its lies. The beat is cold triumph shadowed by doubt.

chapters.title: Signed, Mirabel Kavanagh
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. He testifies under his own name for the first time, surrendering his anonymity and accepting a reprimand for his years of off-book investigating. The old witness, finally told the truth gently, weeps with relief. The beat is cost and release — visibility as both punishment and homecoming.

chapters.title: Day Shift
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV, coda. Months later, Mirabel takes a day-shift job training new dispatchers, his archive now a formal cold-case resource Ruiz consults openly. He mails one last letter — to himself, the first he ever wrote — and finally opens it. The beat is quiet peace: a man who solved the town's secrets learns to live in daylight with his own.
